title: Principles of a cancer operation
subtitle: MDT before knife, margins, nodes, orientation

sources.title: TNM Classification of Malignant Tumours, 8th edition (Brierley JD, Gospodarowicz MK, Wittekind C, eds.)
Localised colon cancer: ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up (Argiles G et al., Ann Oncol)

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Colorectal cancer (NG151)
2017 WSES guidelines on colon and rectal cancer emergencies: obstruction and perforation (Pisano M et al., World J Emerg Surg)

red_flags.text: An elective cancer operation listed without a documented MDT decision.
Staging incomplete, or imaging older than the local standard, or not available in theatre.
No tissue diagnosis where one was obtainable and would change the operation.
An unexpected malignancy found at operation, and the temptation to perform an unplanned radical resection without staging or consent.
A positive margin (R1) or residual disease (R2) not recorded in the operative note or not fed back to the MDT.

do_now.text: Confirm the MDT outcome, the tissue diagnosis and complete staging before the operation; document the planned extent of resection and lymphadenectomy.
Plan for an R0 resection, meaning no residual tumour on microscopy. Know preoperatively which margin is likely to be threatened.
Obtain consent that covers the realistic extensions: stoma, en bloc resection of an adherent organ, conversion, and the possibility that the tumour is unresectable.
Unexpected malignancy at an elective operation: if there is no emergency, biopsy, photograph, document, close, and stage. Do not perform a radical resection the patient has not consented to.
Unexpected malignancy causing the emergency (obstruction, perforation, bleeding): treat the emergency, and where the patient is stable, resect with oncological principles.

assess.text: Fitness for the planned operation, and frailty in the older patient.
Performance status, which determines eligibility for adjuvant treatment and therefore whether the operation achieves its purpose.
Nutritional status before major resection; malnourished patients benefit from preoperative nutritional support.
Thrombosis risk: cancer surgery is high risk and the plan for extended prophylaxis should be made now.

investigate.text: Cross-sectional staging appropriate to the tumour site, and any functional imaging the MDT requests.
Histology or cytology of the primary, and of a suspected metastasis when that would change the treatment.
Tumour markers where they serve as a baseline for follow-up (for example CEA in colorectal cancer).
Completion of luminal assessment where synchronous tumours are possible, such as full colonoscopy before colectomy.

resuscitate.text: Correct anaemia preoperatively where time allows, typically with iron, rather than relying on transfusion.
Prehabilitation and nutrition in the weeks before major surgery when the cancer pathway allows.

definitive.text: Resect with clear margins. R0: no residual tumour. R1: microscopic tumour at the margin. R2: macroscopic tumour left behind. Record your intra-operative assessment of R status.
Perform the lymphadenectomy the tumour requires. Nodal yield matters for staging: for colon cancer at least 12 nodes is the accepted minimum for adequate staging.
Remove adherent structures en bloc rather than separating them: adhesion may be tumour, and dividing it converts an R0 into an R1 resection.
Orient the specimen with sutures or clips, keep it intact, and send it with a request that states the clinical question and neoadjuvant treatment.

escalate.text: Return every resection specimen result to the MDT. An R1 or R2 resection needs a documented plan.
An unexpected malignancy goes to the relevant site-specific MDT, not just to the general surgical list.
Call a specialist colleague intra-operatively when the tumour is beyond your experience; an inadequate first operation cannot be undone.

notes: The first operation is the patient's best chance. A non-radical resection with a positive margin is often not rescued by a second one.
Lymph node yield is partly the surgeon's (a high tie and an intact mesentery) and partly the pathologist's. Both are audited for a reason.
When you find a cancer you did not expect, the safest thing is usually to stop, stage it properly, and come back with consent and a plan.
